extracted.intended_audience: graphic designers, brand and packaging managers, marketers, and design critics evaluating consumer-packaging redesigns
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative checklist for consumer-packaging/brand redesigns, using Tropicana's 2009 redesign as a case study to show what to preserve and what to avoid. Focuses on labeling, information hierarchy, tone, typography, imagery, color, brand messaging, usability/affordances, need for explanatory communications, and commercial consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: Text labeling appears along the top sealed edge and across the front, all knocked out of a large, tactfully positioned block of color indicating the type of juice. Product variations are easily distinguished at a glance.
REDESIGN: Text labeling of the juice type along the top and across the front is inconsistent – one is reversed and one positive – and the thin colored stripe is far less noticeable requiring a greater investment of time and concentration on the part of the shopper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, prominent labeling that indicates product variation at a glance is essential. Anti-patterns include inconsistent treatments (e.g., reversed vs positive), overly thin or hard-to-see color indicators, and placements that force shoppers to search or concentrate more than necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Structure
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: Packaging information is logically structured to make the shopper's selection as efficient as possible. Emphasis is placed first on brand, second on type, and third on supporting information:
Tropicana
No Pulp
Pure Premium, 100% Pure and Natural Orange Juice
REDESIGN: Information structure is inconsiderate of the needs of the shopper. Primary emphasis is wasted on "100% orange" – information that is essentially useless to shoppers who are likely well aware they're looking at orange juice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hierarchy should reflect shopper priorities (brand → product variant → supporting claims). Avoid promoting irrelevant or redundant claims to primary prominence, which confuses or misleads shoppers and reduces selection efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of Voice
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: The product titles No Pulp, Some Pulp, and Lots of Pulp mirror human conversation. By using the same words people use around the house, the brand becomes friendlier, the product more familiar, and the information more comprehensible.
REDESIGN: "Hello, I am a robot. We have a multitude of pulp content levels for you to select from when determining the most appropriate orange-based beverage. Would you prefer High Pulp or Pulp Free?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human, conversational wording that matches how consumers talk about the product; this builds familiarity and comprehension. Anti-patterns are verbose, corporate-speak or overly formal phrasing that alienates or confuses (e.g., "High Pulp" vs the more familiar "Lots of Pulp").

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: The smooth bends and curvatures of the logotype indicate the natural nature of the product. Letter-spaced small caps are indicative of premium quality. Clean, capitalized sans-serifs are crisp and professional. Variations in font sizes are carefully selected and applied consistently.
REDESIGN: Logotype is cold and corporate, lacking any human touch or handcrafted quality. Avant Garde is used everywhere and without any apparent reason. Font weights and sizes are seemingly determined by a dart board. Garnished with a twist of lowercase letter-spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typography should reflect brand personality (natural, handcrafted, premium) and be applied consistently (weights, sizes, spacing). Avoid arbitrary or inappropriate typefaces everywhere, inconsistent sizing/weight decisions, and gimmicky treatments that undermine brand cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: It's practically famous — the juiciest, orangiest orange icon; imagery evokes freshness and taste.
REDESIGN: Bad stock photo of Sunny D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery should be distinctive, high-quality, and reinforce product attributes (freshness, taste, naturalness). Avoid generic or poorly matched stock photos that dilute brand equity and fail to convey the product's desirable qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: Deep, saturated oranges and rich greens inspire the appetite, evoke health, and are reminiscent of the natural world. The box itself looks edible.
REDESIGN: Brighter, more electric colors imply more energetic contents than the original. The yellow juice in the photograph looks washed out and sickly against the overall white box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose color palettes that support product cues (appetite, naturalness, health). Beware that brighter/electric shifts can imply different product attributes; ensure photographic color and background work harmoniously, or the product may appear unappetizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Speak
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: "Why Does Tropicana Taste So Good?" ... [reads paragraph. forms relationship with brand.]
REDESIGN: "Drink In The Spirit of The Morning!" Fits with the energetic color scheme, but sounds like Corporate Ipsum (or ChatGPT, by today's standards). Set on the vertical, no less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand messaging should feel authentic, engaging, and aligned with the product story; avoid generic, clichéd, or corporate-sounding slogans that weaken emotional connection. Also consider placement/legibility (e.g., vertical copy) when evaluating effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affordances
rubrics_metrics.description:
ORIGINAL: You're looking for Orange Pineapple juice in a sea of cartons. Huge purple block and pictures of pineapple make the variant easy to spot; written labels back this up. This design is the pinnacle of user-friendly design.
REDESIGN: Same glass of yellow juice seen on all other cartons – no help there. Thin lime green stripe reminiscent of, um, limes? No pictures of any actual fruit. Yikes. Your only hope is to catch the word "pineapple" somewhere on the box, but it's applied so inconsistently you couldn't possibly know where to look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Packaging should provide clear visual affordances so shoppers can identify variants quickly (distinct color blocks, fruit imagery, consistent label placement). Avoid ambiguous imagery, inconsistent labeling locations, and subtle cues that force shoppers to search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating confusion that requires explanatory outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're ever involved in a redesign process and you come to the conclusion halfway through that you're going to need to dedicate your entire friggin' website to clarifying the situation you're creating (at the time of launch, Tropicana.com had a page dedicated to explaining the new design called 'How do you find Tropicana?'), it's a pretty good indication that you just should cut your losses and start over at square one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A redesign that requires significant explanatory communications (dedicated website pages, extensive PR/education) signals failure in clarity/usability. Designs should stand on their own in retail environments; avoid changes that necessitate post-launch education to prevent shopper confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and reputational impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Years Later... In the short time it existed, their orange juice sales dropped a whopping 20%. In 2011, Peter Arnell left the agency he founded amidst a lawsuit, and Arnell Group closed its doors in 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate redesigns not only on aesthetics but on measurable business outcomes (sales, market share, legal/reputational fallout). Use real-world performance data as a validation: negative sales impact or brand damage are strong signals the redesign failed.
